title: Integration friction maps and competitive tactics for LLM endpoint deals
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note is a compact, field-ready reference for AEs and SEs who are working deals where customers are evaluating hosted LLM APIs vs Redwood (hosted, dedicated, private). Unlike standard feature checklists, this focuses on the realistic integration frictions and the tactical conversation flows that win deals. Use the probes and rebuttals in three phases (starter/technical/procurement) based on where the buyer is in the funnel.

High-level positioning thesis (one-liner, 3 lines):
- One-liner: Redwood gives engineering teams predictable inference economics and operational controls across hosted, reserved and private deployments — so they can ship LLM features without building an ops stack.
- Why it matters: Buying an LLM API is often trivial; shipping and sustaining it in production is where teams hit latency/cost/regulatory landmines.
- Outcome we sell: predictable latency, unit cost controls, and a consistent operational model that survives growth and procurement.

Buyer archetypes and friction map (quick reference):
- Early-stage product engineer (fast proof-of-concept) — friction: SDK ergonomics, rate limits, unclear quotas; motivators: time-to-first-success, sample code, free credits.
- Platform/Infra team (standardize endpoints across org) — friction: multi-team routing, SLA requirements, telemetry gaps; motivators: observability, predictable pricing, private networking.
- Security/Compliance buyer (enterprise) — friction: data residency, key management, audits; motivators: VPC/private deployment, KMS/HSM integration, contract clauses.
- Cost-conscious growth team — friction: unpredictable token spend, tokenization surprises, hidden second-order costs; motivators: per-token breakdown, batching/quantization recommendations.

Conversation playbook: starter -> technical -> procurement
- Starter probes (quick win): "How fast can you get an end-to-end prototype in production? Who owns the inference stack today? How many requests/second in your peak scenario?"
  Suggested starter rebuttal: highlight Redwood quickstart templates, SDK example for <10 minutes to stream a chat, and a standard sample workload for cost estimation.

- Technical probes (dive deeper): "Where do you see token-volume risk? Are you using long-context models or many short requests? Do you need multiregion routing or KV/prefix caching?"
  Technical rebuttal and demo path: show latency SLOs and per-route dashboards, demonstrate prefix/KV caching behavior, and walk through model switch fallback (hosted->dedicated->private). Ask to test with a short prompt set in a show-and-tell.

- Procurement probes (contract/play): "What security controls and contractual SLAs do you require? Is dedicated capacity on the table, or does procurement require a private deployment?"
  Procurement rebuttal: outline Dedicated contract tiers, Private deployment onboarding timeline, and available add-ons (audit logs, retention controls). Provide a one-pager with T&Cs and an SOW template.

Quick competitor snapshots and where to push (field notes):
- Large multi-model API provider (example: OpenAI-like): Strengths: brand recognition, ecosystem integrations, simple dev experience. Weaknesses: opaque unit economics, limited private deployment options, fewer dedicated capacity controls. Push: ask customers to show recent token billing anomalies and request a token-level trace; emphasize Redwood's token-level cost breakdown and batching guidance.

- Anthropic-style safety-first player: Strengths: safety features, curated models. Weaknesses: less transparent perf economics at scale, limited on-prem options. Push: if safety is primary, acknowledge strengths, then pivot to Redwood's observable quality monitoring (evals tied to prompts) and private deployment for regulated workloads.

- Cloud provider endpoint (example: Vertex/Inference-as-service): Strengths: cloud-native integrations, broad infra. Weaknesses: vendor lock-in around data plane, higher ops effort to build inference policies, inconsistent latency at scale. Push: map the customer’s org boundaries and highlight Redwood's unified runtime and routing policies that reduce integration sprawl.

- Open-source-hosted vendors (managed runtimes): Strengths: cost upside, control. Weaknesses: heavy ops burden, patching/optimizing kernels is required, slower time-to-safe-production. Push: frame the decision as build vs buy: Redwood offloads kernel selection, quantization choices, and production tracing so the team's time can be spent on product signals.

Top 8 objections and tactical responses (ranked):
1) "Your price is higher than X."
  - Starter response: acknowledge, then ask about their usage pattern and token churn. Offer to run a token audit/projection and share batching/quantization levers to lower unit cost.
  - Technical add-on: show how caching/batching can reduce effective cost by 20–60% for typical chat workloads.

2) "We can self-host open models cheaper."
  - Starter response: ask what budget they assigned to ongoing ops/personnel. Offer a checklist of hidden costs: kernel engineering, perf regressions, availability/DR, security patches.
  - Procurement: offer a side-by-side TCO over 12 months including SRE FTE assumptions.

3) "We need total data control (on-prem)."
  - Response: validate requirement, then present Redwood Private offering, deployment timeline, and KMS/HSM integration points. Offer a pilot plan with agreed data flows and a basic runbook.

4) "Latency spikes at scale are a concern."
  - Response: present real traces from similar customers, explain batching knobs and autoscale behavior, and propose a stress-test runbook with SRE.

5) "We don’t trust vendor billing accuracy."
  - Response: offer a token-level reconciliation export, show sample audit logs and the per-route cost breakdown feature.

6) "We need specific model variants or quantization types."
  - Response: confirm supported architectures, discuss model onboarding process, and explain Redwood's kernel-mapper and quantization recommendation process (we run platform-grade validation before serving).

7) "We’re already embedded with a cloud vendor."
  - Response: emphasize multi-cloud routing and the ability to deploy private/restricted endpoints that connect back to cloud infra. Sell the control plane benefits and reduced cross-team friction.

8) "How are you different from X?"
  - Response pattern: 1) validate the competitor strength, 2) call out the operational gap (e.g., no dedicated capacity SLAs, no per-token attribution), 3) offer a technical demo targeted to that gap.

Traps to set for competing vendors (tactical guidance for SEs):
- Ask for a live token reconciliation for the month; if they can’t provide one, highlight risk to forecasting.
- Ask the competitor how they handle prefix/KV cache invalidation and request examples; lack of clear answers indicates poor production maturity.
- Push them on fallback modes: if model A is overloaded what happens — handoff to lower-cost variants? If ambiguity, position Redwood’s automated fallback routing and canary rollouts.
- Probe for observability: do they expose per-request traces, per-route token counts, caller-level latencies? If not, claim Redwood's console as a compliance and debugging advantage.

Demo flow (10–15 minute technical proof):
1) Short intro & problem statement (1 min)
2) Live demo: spin up a hosted endpoint, run a 5–10 prompt evaluation, show latency and token breakdown (5 min)
3) Show fallback: simulate capacity pressure and show automatic model switch (2 min)
4) Show private/dedicated slide: timeline and controls (2 min)
5) Ask for next step: pilot scope and target metrics (1 min)

Deal signals checklist (what to look for in discovery):
- They ask about "predictable unit economics" or "token-level logs".
- They ask for private networking or KMS/HSM.
- They want guaranteed p99 latency targets or mention tail latency problems.
- Multiple teams are consuming the API (signals platform need).

Useful soundbites for reps: (short and punchy)
- "We don't just give you models — we give you predictable inference economics and the ops to keep it stable."
- "Ship faster today, avoid an operations rebuild next quarter."
- "If you want to treat inference like a commodity, you'll pay for the surprises — we aim to remove them."

Appendix: one-page pilot template (boilerplate)
- Goal: validate latency, cost, and observability for specific workload.
- Duration: 4 weeks
- Scope: N model variants, X qps baseline, Y peak qps, sample prompt set (attached).
- Success criteria: p50/p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens under threshold, telemetry completeness (per-request tokens, traces).
- Deliverables: onboarding guide, weekly checkpoint, final TCO report.

Field notes and open questions:
- Track any deals where competitors promise "free dedicated capacity" — rare but exists; ask for contractual proof and SLA details.
- Capture any vendor admissions about billing opacity; this is a repeatable win-theme.
- Open: build a short script that extracts per-route token anomalies from our console to share as blinded examples in sales cycles.

Use this doc as a living artifact. SEs, AEs: please add anonymized deal anecdotes (what competitor said verbatim, what we said, and the outcome) into the linked Confluence page so we can iterate on rebuttals and traps.
